cards.front: In a typical dividing eukaryotic cell, what happens in G1, in S and in G2?
cards.back: G1: the cell grows, makes proteins and does its everyday work. S: it copies its DNA. G2: it makes proteins that will move the chromosomes and gets ready to divide.
cards.quote: In G1 the cell grows, makes proteins and does its everyday work.

cards.front: A student says cells in interphase are resting. What is wrong with that idea?
cards.back: Interphase is the part between divisions, and it is not a rest. The cell grows, copies its DNA and prepares to divide.
cards.why: G1, S and G2 are all interphase.
cards.quote: Interphase is the part between divisions.

cards.front: DNA is stored in {{c1::chromosomes}}, long strands of DNA wrapped around proteins.
cards.quote: DNA is stored in chromosomes, long strands of DNA wrapped around proteins.

cards.front: After S phase, each chromosome has been copied. Each copy is a {{c1::sister chromatid}}.
cards.back: The two copies stay joined until they separate.
cards.quote: After S phase, each chromosome has been copied. Each copy is a sister chromatid.

cards.front: Why must a cell copy its chromosomes before mitosis?
cards.back: So that each new nucleus can get one full set. The rule: copy each chromosome first, then separate the copies.
cards.why: This is the lesson's copy-then-separate rule.
cards.quote: Copy each chromosome first; separate the copies so each nucleus gets one.

cards.front: A typical human body cell with a nucleus has 46 chromosomes before S phase. How many chromosomes and sister chromatids does it have right after S phase, and how many in each new nucleus after mitosis?
cards.back: After S: 46 copied chromosomes and 92 sister chromatids. Each new nucleus: 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids. Copying doubles the DNA molecules, not the number of joined chromosome units.
cards.quote: A typical human body cell with a nucleus has 46 chromosomes.

cards.front: What is the difference between mitosis and cytokinesis?
cards.back: Mitosis divides the nucleus into two nuclei, each with a full set of chromosomes. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, which splits one cell into two.
cards.quote: Mitosis is the division of the nucleus into two nuclei, each with a full set of chromosomes.

cards.front: What happens when the controls on the cell cycle fail?
cards.back: Cells can keep dividing when they should not. This uncontrolled division is a key feature of cancer.
cards.quote: When the controls on the cycle fail, cells can keep dividing when they should not.

cards.front: What is the centromere?
cards.back: A narrow region of a chromosome where the two sister chromatids are held together.
cards.quote: Sister chromatids are held together at the centromere, a narrow region of the chromosome.

cards.front: {{c1::Spindle fibers}} are thin protein fibers that attach to chromosomes and move them.
cards.quote: Spindle fibers are thin protein fibers that attach to chromosomes and move them.

cards.front: On a stained slide, a cell shows thick, separate chromosomes. Which stage is it, and what has happened?
cards.back: Prophase. The chromosomes have coiled up. Spindle fibers form, and near the end the nuclear envelope breaks down.
cards.quote: The chromosomes have coiled up. Spindle fibers form, and near the end the nuclear envelope breaks down.

cards.front: On a stained slide, the copied chromosomes form one row across the middle of the cell. Which stage is it, and what put them there?
cards.back: Metaphase. Spindle fibers have lined the chromosomes up before separation.
cards.quote: Spindle fibers have lined them up before separation.

cards.front: A human cell is in anaphase. Its sister chromatids have separated. How many chromosomes does the whole cell hold at this moment, and why?
cards.back: 92 chromosomes. Each separated sister chromatid is now its own chromosome. Each end of the cell will then form a nucleus with 46.
cards.why: Rests on the 46-chromosome, 92-chromatid count after S phase.
cards.quote: Sister chromatids have separated and are being pulled to opposite ends. Each is now its own chromosome.

cards.front: What does a cell show in telophase?
cards.back: A chromosome set sits at each end as two nuclei appear. A new nuclear envelope forms around each set, and the chromosomes loosen again.
cards.quote: A new nuclear envelope forms around each set, and the chromosomes loosen again.

cards.front: How does cytokinesis differ in an animal cell and a plant cell, and why?
cards.back: An animal cell pinches in two with a furrow. A plant cell has a stiff wall that cannot pinch, so a cell plate grows outward from the middle and becomes a new wall.
cards.quote: A plant cell's stiff wall cannot pinch, so a cell plate grows outward from the middle until it becomes a new wall.

cards.front: A stained plant cell has two new nuclei and a plate growing across its middle. Has mitosis finished, has cytokinesis finished, or has only one finished?
cards.back: Mitosis has finished because two nuclei have formed. Cytokinesis is still underway because the cell plate has not yet become a complete wall.
cards.quote: A stained plant cell has two new nuclei and a plate growing across its middle. Has mitosis finished, has cytokinesis finished, or has only one finished?

cards.front: Name four reasons cells divide.
cards.back: Growth, repair, replacement of lost cells, and asexual reproduction.
cards.quote: Both depend on adding cells, and cells divide for several reasons.
cards.section: Explain: why cells divide and stay small

cards.front: Why does a cell's membrane matter for how big the cell can get?
cards.back: Oxygen, food molecules and wastes all cross the cell membrane. A cell needs enough surface for the amount of inside it has.
cards.quote: Oxygen, food molecules and wastes all cross the cell membrane, which you study in Crossing the Membrane.
cards.section: Explain: why cells divide and stay small

cards.front: In the cube model of a cell, what happens to surface area and volume each time the side doubles, and what does that mean for a large cell?
cards.back: Volume grows eight times, surface area only four times. A large cell has less membrane for each bit of its inside.
cards.quote: Each time the side doubles, volume grows eight times but surface only four times, so a large cell has less membrane for each bit of its inside.
cards.section: Explain: why cells divide and stay small

cards.front: In the cube model of a cell, what is the surface area divided by volume for a cube with a side of 3 units?
cards.back: Surface area = 6 x 3 x 3 = 54. Volume = 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. The ratio is 54 / 27 = 2, between the 3 for side 2 and the 1.5 for side 4.
cards.quote: These values come from geometry (area = 6 × side × side, volume = side × side × side), not from measuring cells.
cards.section: Explain: why cells divide and stay small

cards.front: In the cube model, a cube cell with a side of 4 units is replaced by eight cubes with a side of 2 units each, which hold the same total volume. Compare the total surface area and the surface area per unit of volume. What does this suggest about dividing?
cards.back: One 4-unit cube: surface 96, ratio 1.5. Eight 2-unit cubes: surface 8 x 24 = 192, total volume 64, ratio 3. Smaller cells have more surface for each unit of volume. Real cells are not cubes, so this is a model comparison.
cards.why: Rests on the cube values: side 2 gives 24 and 8, side 4 gives 96 and 64.
cards.quote: Key idea: Cells divide to grow, repair, replace and reproduce. One reason they stay small is that a bigger cell has less surface for each unit of volume.
cards.section: Explain: why cells divide and stay small

cards.front: How does an onion root grow deeper into the soil?
cards.back: Cells near the tip divide. Just behind that zone, the new cells grow longer, and that lengthening pushes the root through the soil.
cards.quote: Near the tip, cells divide. Just behind that zone, the new cells grow longer, and that lengthening pushes the root through the soil.
cards.section: Explain: why cells divide and stay small

cards.front: In a count of 36 onion root-tip cells, 3 are in metaphase. Assuming one cycle takes 24 hours, estimate the time in metaphase.
cards.back: 3/36 of 1,440 minutes = 120 minutes, or about 2 hours. This is a model result, not a measured time.
cards.quote: Estimate the time in metaphase as its fraction times 1,440 minutes.

cards.front: In the same count of 36 onion root-tip cells, 20 are in interphase. Assuming a 24-hour cycle, estimate the time in interphase.
cards.back: 20/36 of 1,440 minutes = 800 minutes, or about 13.3 hours. Interphase holds the most cells, so it gets the longest time estimate.
cards.quote: Which phase holds the most cells? About what fraction of the cells is it?

cards.front: A set of onion root-tip photographs may have been chosen to show every stage of mitosis. Would a randomly picked field probably show more or fewer interphase cells, and how would that change the phase-time estimates?
cards.back: More interphase cells. Interphase would then get a larger fraction and a longer time estimate, and the mitosis phases would get smaller ones.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that a phase's time estimate is its fraction of cells times the cycle length.
cards.quote: The activity does not say how these photographs were picked, and they may have been chosen to show every stage.

cards.front: Warmer onion roots show a larger fraction of tip cells in mitosis. Can that result alone tell you the total cycle length?
cards.back: No. The result would suggest that temperature changes the cycle, but a total cycle length needs a separate measurement.
cards.quote: If warmer roots show a larger fraction of cells in mitosis, can that result alone tell you the total cycle length?

cards.front: You test whether onion roots grown warmer have a larger fraction of tip cells in mitosis. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control.
cards.back: Independent variable: growing temperature, checked with a thermometer. Dependent variable: the fraction of tip cells in any stage of mitosis. Control: roots grown at ordinary room temperature.
cards.quote: Independent variable: the growing temperature, for example a cool room and a warmer incubator, checked with a thermometer.

cards.front: When counting cells on a root-tip slide, why count every cell in a row of fields instead of only the interesting ones?
cards.back: Picking only dividing cells would bias the fraction toward mitosis. Counting every cell in a row of fields, up to a few hundred, gives a fair sample.
cards.quote: On each slide, count every cell in a row of fields, not only interesting ones, until you have a few hundred.
